title: PostgreSQL DBA Series: What a DBA Actually Does

lines.say: What does a PostgreSQL DBA really do every day?
lines.cap: What does a *PostgreSQL* *DBA* really do every day?

lines.say: This is episode one of a one hundred and forty episode PostgreSQL DBA series, from the basics all the way to production.
lines.cap: Episode 1 of a *140-episode* PostgreSQL DBA series, basics to *production.*

lines.say: In one line: a DBA keeps the database available, secure, fast and recoverable, and ready to grow.
lines.cap: A DBA keeps the database *available,* *secure,* *fast* and *recoverable.*

lines.say: Availability. The database has to be up whenever the application needs it, so the DBA monitors it, sets up replication and plans for failures.
lines.cap: *Availability:* up whenever the app needs it. Monitoring, *replication,* a plan for failures.

lines.say: Security. The DBA controls who can connect, and what each role is allowed to read or change.
lines.cap: *Security:* who can connect, and what each *role* can read or change.

lines.say: Performance. Find the slow queries, read their plans, and tune indexes and settings.
lines.cap: *Performance:* find slow queries, read plans, tune *indexes* and settings.

lines.say: Backups. Take them on a schedule, and keep copies somewhere safe.
lines.cap: *Backups:* on a schedule, with copies kept *safe.*

lines.say: Recovery. This is the one people forget. A backup only counts if you can restore it, so practise restores.
lines.cap: *Recovery:* a backup only counts if you can *restore* it.

lines.say: Capacity. Watch disk space, connections and data growth, before they turn into an outage.
lines.cap: *Capacity:* watch disk, connections and growth *before* they become an outage.

lines.say: PostgreSQL also needs routine maintenance. VACUUM reclaims space from updated and deleted rows, and keeps the planner's statistics fresh.
lines.cap: *VACUUM* reclaims space from updated and deleted rows, and refreshes *statistics.*

lines.say: Then upgrades. The PostgreSQL project recommends always running the current minor release, because minor releases carry bug and security fixes.
lines.cap: Run the current *minor* *release.* It carries bug and *security* fixes.

lines.say: A new major version arrives about once a year, and each one is supported for five years.
lines.cap: A new *major* version about once a year, supported for *5* *years.*

lines.say: Here's a simple morning check you can follow.
lines.cap: Here's a simple *morning* *check* you can follow.

lines.say: First, check that every server is up, and that replicas are keeping up.
Next, look at disk space, connection counts and long-running queries.
Then confirm that last night's backup actually succeeded.
After that comes the planned work: tuning, access requests and changes.
Commands are easy to look up. Understanding what PostgreSQL does inside is what this series builds, one episode at a time.
lines.cap: Understand what PostgreSQL does *inside.* That's what this series builds.

lines.say: Tomorrow: database versus DBMS versus SQL. Follow so you don't miss it, and send this to a friend who wants to become a DBA.
lines.cap: Tomorrow: database vs *DBMS* vs *SQL.* *Follow* and send this to a friend.
